title: Implicit Conversions Kill Index Seeks
description: Comparing an indexed string column to a number makes SQL Server convert every row and abandon the index; match the literal's type to keep the seek. Why it matters: type mismatches between application code and the database schema are extremely common (especially with ORMs) and silently defeat indexes without any error or warning.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson is about a sneaky performance killer: comparing two values of different data types, and having SQL Server silently convert one of them behind the scenes. This is called an **implicit conversion**, and it can quietly disable an otherwise perfectly good index.

Why does this happen? SQL Server has a fixed pecking order for data types, called **data type precedence**. When you compare a text column to a number, SQL Server always converts the *text* side to a number to make the comparison fair — it never goes the other way. That sounds harmless, but if you write `WHERE AccountCode = 1050000` and `AccountCode` is actually stored as text, SQL Server can't just convert your literal `1050000` — it decides it must convert *every single value in the column* to a number first, before it can compare anything.

Here's the mental model: imagine your index is a sorted list of phone numbers stored as text, like "011-555-0142". Now imagine someone asks the database to treat every single entry as if it were a plain number first, and only then compare it. To do that "translate first" step, the database can no longer trust the original sorted order — it has to re-check and convert every row, one at a time, which throws away the index's whole advantage. The fix is simple: match your literal's type to the column's actual type, so no row-by-row conversion is needed.

## Scenario
`AccountCode` is a `VARCHAR(20)` column with an index on it. A developer queries `WHERE AccountCode = 1050000` (an **integer** literal). The query scans 250k rows and the plan shows a yellow warning.

## Why it's slow
When you compare a `VARCHAR` column to an `INT`, SQL Server follows **data-type precedence**: `INT` outranks `VARCHAR`, so it converts the **column** to `INT` on every row — `CONVERT_IMPLICIT(int, AccountCode)`. That function-on-the-column makes the predicate non-sargable, so the index can't seek. The plan shows an **implicit conversion / CONVERT_IMPLICIT** warning.

## What to look for
- A scan instead of a seek, plus a **type-conversion warning** on the operator.
- `CONVERT_IMPLICIT` in the Seek/Scan predicate text.

## The concept
Match the literal's type to the column: quote it as a string `'1050000'`. Better yet, fix the schema so codes are stored in the right type. With a matching type the `AccountCode` index seeks directly.
hints: Note the yellow warning on the operator — what type conversion is happening?
AccountCode is VARCHAR but the literal 1050000 is INT; INT has higher precedence so the COLUMN gets converted.
Quote the literal so it matches the column type: WHERE AccountCode = '1050000'.
